why: The contract between the two guards. test_guard.py asserts that the Python removal of the
vertex entry direction clause produces exactly the rings this table records, and
test-guard.mjs asserts the same of the JavaScript one, so a case added here constrains both.
The guard exists because a check that has only ever passed is half a check. It removes the
clause from the library's OUTPUT rather than from its source, because the corpus cannot reach
into either library and must ask the same question of both. For this clause the undoing is
exact: the clause reverses a ring while holding its first vertex, so applying it twice is
The table matters most for JavaScript, where the runner's library call is not wired up yet.
Until it is, this is the only thing asserting that the two guards remove the same clause.
THE FIRST VERTEX STAYS WHERE IT IS in every reversed case below. A guard that reversed the
whole list would renormalise the starting vertex as a side effect, the check's ring comparison
is insensitive to where a ring starts, and the difference would therefore never be seen.
Coordinates are metres. The base ring is the 4 m by 3 m rectangle in the y = 0 plane that
ring_fixtures.json uses, so the two tables can be read side by side.

note: Measured on the committed fixture with the clause removed: all eight surfaces disagree and
the worst is 4.0000 m. The guard requires at least this, so that a clause reduced to a
rounding difference fails rather than passes.
